title: New Beginnings

jokes.text: Leslie insists on interviewing for her own job, treating it as a formal process despite Ron being her former boss who walked her down the aisle
jokes.setup: Leslie arrives to interview for the Deputy Parks Director job — a job that was already hers
jokes.punchline: Ron points out he was her boss AND walked her down the aisle, making the formal interview theater absurd
jokes.explanation: This is a perfect distillation of Leslie's character — her obsessive love of process and fairness taken to absurd extremes. Ron walking her down the aisle detail is a genuine laugh-out-loud escalation. Strong character integration because ONLY Leslie would demand to interview for her own job.

dialogue.speaker: Leslie
dialogue.line: I know this job is already mine, but I want to do the interview anyway. It's protocol.

dialogue.speaker: Ron
dialogue.line: Leslie, you're the director. You don't need to interview yourself.

dialogue.speaker: Leslie
dialogue.line: Ron, rules exist for a reason. What if I didn't follow procedure? What kind of government would we have?

dialogue.speaker: Ron
dialogue.line: A functional one.

dialogue.speaker: Leslie
dialogue.line: I'm going to need you to schedule that interview. And I'll need three copies of my resume, notarized.

jokes.text: "What do you believe should be the ultimate goal of this department?" / Leslie launches into the ancient Greek agora speech
jokes.setup: Ron reluctantly agrees to conduct a real interview
jokes.punchline: Leslie immediately over-answers the first question with an academic monologue, undermining her own request for professionalism
jokes.explanation: Classic Leslie over-preparation joke. The mid-speech interruption 'What are you writing? Is it good?' is a perfectly timed crack in her composure and very funny — she can't even get through her own performance without breaking.

dialogue.speaker: Leslie
dialogue.line: My entire premise was demanding equal treatment.

dialogue.speaker: Leslie
dialogue.line: But you know what? Forget that. I'm just going to abandon my principles when they don't work in my favor.

jokes.text: "The correct answer is 'Give it all back to the taxpayers.'" / Ron declares their philosophies fundamentally incompatible
jokes.setup: Ron asks about best use of the yearly budget in a mock interview
jokes.punchline: He reveals his libertarian answer — which is to abolish the department's entire purpose — and frames it as if it's the objectively correct answer
jokes.explanation: Strong character integration — Ron's libertarianism expressed through a job interview he didn't want to conduct. The follow-up 'It's a miracle we ever worked together without killing each other' is a perfect button that Ron would never normally say, which makes it funny.

dialogue.speaker: Ron
dialogue.line: I've known Leslie for years. I've watched her grow as a person and as a public servant. I've seen her at her best and at her worst. I was there when she got her first job at the Parks Department. I've watched her navigate complex political situations. I've seen her fight for what she believes in, sometimes against all odds.

dialogue.speaker: Ron
dialogue.line: And I was there the night she cried in my office because she thought she'd never find love.

jokes.text: It seems you and I have fundamentally different philosophies. Frankly, it's a miracle we ever worked together without killing each other. Good day.
jokes.setup: Ron has been Leslie's closest work ally for years; they have a deep, warm friendship
jokes.punchline: Ron plays the formal interview game so completely he declares it a 'miracle' they survived each other — with total deadpan sincerity
jokes.explanation: Works as an extension of the running bit — Ron has fully committed to the bit. 'Good day' as a dismissal in this context is a nice touch. The irony of Ron calling their legendary friendship a 'miracle they didn't kill each other' lands because the audience knows how close they are.

dialogue.speaker: Leslie
dialogue.line: Ron, what are your budget priorities?

dialogue.speaker: Ron
dialogue.line: I'd like to cut the Parks Department budget by 90 percent. Eliminate unnecessary positions. And fire everyone.

jokes.text: "Give me special treatment." — Leslie drops all pretense and demands what she wanted in the first place
jokes.setup: Leslie spent the entire cold open demanding to be treated like everyone else
jokes.punchline: She immediately abandons that position and asks for special treatment the moment the interview doesn't go her way
jokes.explanation: Tight callback to the cold open's premise. The entire opening scene is a setup for this single line. Exceptional economy — four words pay off two minutes of buildup. Leslie's hypocrisy is endearing rather than cynical, which keeps the joke warm.

dialogue.speaker: Ron Swanson
dialogue.line: A spirit animal is not something to be assigned lightly. This is a bureaucratic process with no appeals.

dialogue.speaker: Leslie Knope
dialogue.line: But Ron, don't you think people should have a say in their own spirit animal?

dialogue.speaker: Ron Swanson
dialogue.line: No. The committee has spoken. There is no appeals process.

jokes.text: "You guys think I'm a border collie?" / "So obviously a cocker spaniel. The spirit dog committee ruled on that weeks ago. There is no appeals process."
jokes.setup: Leslie objects to her spirit dog assignment
jokes.punchline: The office has a fully bureaucratized spirit dog committee with official rulings and no appeals process — mirroring Leslie's own government obsession
jokes.explanation: The joke has elegant irony — the committee structure satirizes Leslie's governing style. 'There is no appeals process' delivered deadpan is very funny and feels true to how this office would operate in her absence/image.

dialogue.speaker: Leslie
dialogue.line: My spirit animal is a dog? A DOG? I'm obviously a bald eagle or a wolf or some kind of majestic tiger.

dialogue.speaker: Leslie
dialogue.line: Wait, actually, a dog is perfect. Dogs are loyal, hardworking, and they never give up. That's exactly who I am.

jokes.text: "Classic border collie. Has to control everything." — talking head comment after Leslie tries to redirect the meeting
jokes.setup: Leslie tries to move the meeting away from spirit dogs
jokes.punchline: Tom's talking head confirms the border collie assessment by using her own behavior as evidence
jokes.explanation: Perfect mockumentary structure — the confessional comment is funnier because it immediately follows and validates the joke. The circular logic (her protesting proves she's a border collie) is satisfying comedy architecture.

dialogue.speaker: Leslie
dialogue.line: Okay, can we please get back to the actual agenda? We have a lot of work to do.

dialogue.speaker: Ben
dialogue.line: Leslie, I think what you're doing right now is classic Anxious Squirrel behavior.

dialogue.speaker: Leslie
dialogue.line: What? No, I'm not—

dialogue.speaker: Tom
dialogue.line: Yeah, and you're clearly in Defensive Peacock mode.

dialogue.speaker: April
dialogue.line: Everyone knows Leslie's spirit animal is Ambitious Beaver. She can't help it.

jokes.text: "Can I get a what-what?" / "What?" / "What?" / "Thank you."
jokes.setup: Tom asks for crowd energy on his lemonade stand news
jokes.punchline: Everyone responds with confused 'What?' questions rather than hype, and Tom accepts them as sufficient
jokes.explanation: Tight three-beat joke. Tom's social currency doesn't translate in this room; the confusion 'What?' being accepted as a 'what-what' is excellent economy. Very quotable exchange.

dialogue.speaker: Tom
dialogue.line: Guys, we crushed it. Can you please acknowledge my victory by giving me some dap?

dialogue.speaker: Ben
dialogue.line: Oh, sure.

dialogue.speaker: Ben
dialogue.line: Here's the contact information for a dap contractor in the area.

jokes.text: Tom shows off the app that pops champagne whenever he says something awesome, then the joke is it cost $9
jokes.setup: Tom announces a flashy app that celebrates his statements
jokes.punchline: "It was only 9 bucks" — the deflation from cool-guy tech to bargain-bin price
jokes.explanation: Classic Tom joke — the self-aggrandizing tech enthusiasm punctured by the mundane price point. Character-specific but fairly well-worn territory for Tom.

dialogue.speaker: Tom
dialogue.line: I created an app called 'Humble Brag.' It's like Twitter, but every post is automatically prefaced with 'I'm so blessed' or 'Living my best life.' It's the most narcissistic thing I've ever made, and I made it specifically so people could celebrate their own statements without any self-awareness whatsoever.

jokes.text: Larry's only contribution to the meeting is straightening a picture frame on the wall
jokes.setup: Leslie tells Larry there's nothing he can do to help with the lemonade project
jokes.punchline: Larry finds the one tiny useless thing he can contribute — straightening a frame — and does so with dignity
jokes.explanation: Wordless physical comedy. Larry's pathetic contribution — and apparent satisfaction with it — is earned by years of character building. The 'Oh, Larry.' sigh from Leslie perfectly frames it. Strong visual punchline.

dialogue.speaker: Leslie
dialogue.line: Well, I may not be able to solve all your problems, but I can be here for you in the most technically minimal way possible.

dialogue.speaker: Leslie
dialogue.line: I will sit near you. Not next to you, because that would be too helpful. But in the general vicinity.

dialogue.speaker: Leslie
dialogue.line: I'll even make eye contact if you really need it. Occasionally.

jokes.text: "Oh, Larry." — Leslie's weary reaction to Larry straightening the picture
jokes.setup: Larry has just done something pathetically small and unhelpful
jokes.punchline: The entire joke is Leslie's two-word exasperated response — a catchphrase-level moment
jokes.explanation: Two words delivering the full joke is excellent economy. The joke is mostly about what's NOT said — the accumulated history of Leslie's patience with Larry lives in that 'Oh.' Running gag energy.

dialogue.speaker: Leslie
dialogue.line: I can help you with your research.

dialogue.speaker: Tom
dialogue.line: No thanks, Lil' Sebastian's mom. I got this.

jokes.text: Chris and Ann have been photographing locations in City Hall where they met for their unborn baby — then Chris impulsively proposes because Larry's speech went on forever
jokes.setup: Larry begins a long, earnest speech about love and couples who look at each other a certain way
jokes.punchline: Chris proposes mid-sentence just to end Larry's speech: 'That literally went on forever. I thought you were never gonna stop talking. But now that you have... Ann Perkins, will you marry me?'
jokes.explanation: This is the standout joke of the episode. The setup exploits Larry's well-established tendency to ramble sentimentally. The punchline weaponizes that — Chris proposes not from inspiration but from desperation to escape Larry's monologue. 'That literally went on forever. I thought you were never gonna stop talking. But now that you have...' is a masterfully constructed pivot. The romanticism and the insult coexist perfectly. Easily the most memorable moment in the episode and justifies 8+ scoring.

dialogue.speaker: Larry
dialogue.line: Love is the most beautiful thing in the world. It's what makes us human, what connects us to each other in ways that transcend logic and reason.

dialogue.speaker: Chris
dialogue.line: Actually, that's not true. Love is just a series of chemical reactions in your brain designed to make you procreate. Also, you have a stain on your shirt.

jokes.text: Say, when are you crazy kids gonna get hitched? / Well, you know, actually, we haven't discussed it in a while. No, it's kind of taken a back seat.
jokes.setup: Larry asks an innocent, grandmotherly question about marriage
jokes.punchline: The revelation that two people expecting a child and planning to move to a new city together have not discussed marriage — and the slight awkwardness between them as they admit it
jokes.explanation: Functional setup for the episode's Chris/Ann storyline. Larry as the inadvertent catalyst for a relationship conversation is appropriate. Mild comedic value on its own but important structurally.

dialogue.speaker: Ben
dialogue.line: Ann, you make me the happiest man alive. Will you marry me?

dialogue.speaker: Ann
dialogue.line: *chokes on crackers* Yes! Yes, I— *cough cough* —I will marry you!

jokes.text: "Wow." / "Cracker dust." — Ann's response to Chris's proposal is to choke on a cracker
jokes.setup: Chris has just proposed marriage
jokes.punchline: Ann's romantic response is interrupted by her coughing on a cracker, reducing the moment to physical comedy
jokes.explanation: 'Cracker dust' as a response to a marriage proposal is genuinely funny. Deflates the romance in a very specific physical way. The escalating cracker comedy across the scene works well.

dialogue.speaker: Chris
dialogue.line: I have to say, that proposal was a lot like my digestive system. Unexpected, a little messy, and ultimately successful.

jokes.text: "Oh, no, no, no. I'm a bit of a germaphobe." — Chris refuses to share water with Ann mid-proposal
jokes.setup: Ann asks to sip Chris's water while choking
jokes.punchline: Chris, having just proposed, reveals germaphobia and refuses — even as she's literally coughing
jokes.explanation: Character-specific joke — Chris Traeger's health obsession making him refuse to share water at the worst possible romantic moment. The contrast between 'will you marry me' and 'I'm a germaphobe' is a perfect tonal collision.

dialogue.speaker: Ben
dialogue.line: So I may have acquired some cheese that's technically not legal to import into the country, but it's from this amazing fromagerie in France, and I thought you all deserved to try it.

dialogue.speaker: Ben
dialogue.line: I mean, it's not like I'm smuggling heroin or anything. It's just cheese. Delicious, creamy, probably fine cheese. The FDA is very conservative about these things anyway.

dialogue.speaker: Ben
dialogue.line: You know what? Forget I said anything. It's cheese.

jokes.text: "No part of this is how I pictured it. I thought another cracker might push it through, but I was wrong." — Ann's talking head on the proposal
jokes.setup: The proposal scene was chaotic, unglamorous, and involved Larry and cracker-choking
jokes.punchline: Ann's assessment — deadpan — is that she hoped a second cracker would solve the problem
jokes.explanation: Excellent confessional beat. The logic that a second cracker would help is absurdist but feels completely true to the moment. The flat delivery of 'I was wrong' against the romantic context is a very strong deadpan joke. High quotability.

dialogue.speaker: Ben
dialogue.line: I'm so excited about this project! We're going to make such a positive impact on the community.

dialogue.speaker: April
dialogue.line: So what you're saying is we're all going to die. I volunteer as tribute.

jokes.text: "Hello, France!" — Ben introduces illegal French cheese to the office as a friendly opener on his first day as city manager
jokes.setup: Ben wants to seem like a warm, approachable boss on his first day
jokes.punchline: He's brought in contraband — illegally imported unpasteurized cheese — as his icebreaker gift
jokes.explanation: Premise joke that pays off bigger later with the police. Ben's obliviousness to the illegality while trying to seem cool is good character work. Setup for a running gag.

dialogue.speaker: Ben
dialogue.line: Listen, I need to be firm here. You all need to follow protocol.

dialogue.speaker: Ben
dialogue.line: But I really appreciate what you're trying to do, and I think you're all great people.

dialogue.speaker: Ben
dialogue.line: So this is non-negotiable. No exceptions.

dialogue.speaker: Ben
dialogue.line: Though I completely understand why you might want to bend the rules, and honestly, I respect that.

dialogue.speaker: Ben
dialogue.line: But you can't. I won't allow it.

dialogue.speaker: Ben
dialogue.line: You're all wonderful and I love working with you.

jokes.text: "What the hell is wrong with you? Are you in a cult? Can I join? Let's sacrifice Larry."
jokes.setup: Ben gives an enthusiastic open-door-policy speech about wanting to be friends and a boss
jokes.punchline: April's immediate response is to accuse him of being in a cult and suggest sacrificing Larry
jokes.explanation: Three escalating beats in rapid succession — cult accusation, wanting to join, sacrifice Larry — is excellent April characterization. The pivot from 'are you in a cult' to 'can I join' subverts the expected judgment. Larry's name-drop as sacrifice is economical cruelty. Very quotable.

dialogue.speaker: Ben
dialogue.line: Did you know that under the new bathroom break time limits, some employees have started showering at work?

dialogue.speaker: Leslie
dialogue.line: What? That's insane! Where are they even showering?

dialogue.speaker: Ben
dialogue.line: In the bathroom. Where else would they shower?

dialogue.speaker: Leslie
dialogue.line: Ben, there's no shower in our bathroom.

dialogue.speaker: Ben
dialogue.line: Not with that attitude.

jokes.text: "Everyone is the best. We're cutting vacation time. Let's eat vitamins. This is exhausting." — Ben's talking head on having to play both nice guy and hammer
jokes.setup: Ben explains he has to combine Chris's relentless positivity with his own disciplinarian style
jokes.punchline: The rapid-fire combination of affirmations and terrible news, ending with 'This is exhausting'
jokes.explanation: Compact, well-structured talking head. The juxtaposition of Chris-style enthusiasm with budget cuts is inherently funny, but 'This is exhausting' as the button is the perfect landing. Ben's deadpan exhaustion is perfectly character-integrated. Justifies 8+ — it's a well-observed piece of workplace comedy with strong economy.

dialogue.speaker: Ben Wyatt
dialogue.line: I'm going to need everyone to work harder, but also take more time off. Be more creative, but follow the rules exactly. Think outside the box, but stay in your lane.

dialogue.speaker: Tom Haverford
dialogue.line: So what you're saying is you're having a mental breakdown?

dialogue.speaker: Ben Wyatt
dialogue.line: No, I'm being a dynamic leader.

dialogue.speaker: Tom Haverford
dialogue.line: Those are the same thing.

jokes.text: "That's not fair, my cell phone is how I avoid doing work." — employee responds to cell phone ban
jokes.setup: Ben announces no cell phone usage on City Hall property
jokes.punchline: An employee openly admits phones are how they avoid working — complete candor about workplace loafing
jokes.explanation: Functional observational joke about workplace productivity. The honesty is the punchline but it's not particularly novel territory. Good economy, weak originality.

dialogue.speaker: Jerry
dialogue.line: New rule: bathroom breaks are limited to five minutes.

dialogue.speaker: Tom
dialogue.line: Five minutes? What am I supposed to do, just pee and leave? What about washing my hands? What about a little primping in the mirror?

dialogue.speaker: Jerry
dialogue.line: Those are all part of the five minutes.

dialogue.speaker: Tom
dialogue.line: Well, what about a shower?

dialogue.speaker: Leslie
dialogue.line: A shower?

dialogue.speaker: Tom
dialogue.line: Yeah, you know, to freshen up.

dialogue.speaker: Ron
dialogue.line: Tom, we work in an office. Not a gym. Not a spa. An office.

jokes.text: "Bathroom breaks should be limited to five minutes?" / "I can't shower in five minutes."
jokes.setup: Ben announces bathroom break time limits
jokes.punchline: The employee reveals he showers at work — raising more questions than the rule answers
jokes.explanation: Nice escalation from 'avoiding work' to 'literally showering at work.' The implication is funnier than the explicit line — this government office is a complete disaster. Good economy.

dialogue.speaker: Tom
dialogue.line: I've developed a comprehensive spirit animal classification system based on kangaroos.

dialogue.speaker: Tom
dialogue.line: You answer a few key questions about yourself, and boom—you get paired with your perfect kangaroo spirit animal.

dialogue.speaker: Tom
dialogue.line: It's foolproof. Well, it would be if there were more than three kangaroos.

jokes.text: "See, he's acting all loosey-goosey, but that little dude's wound so tight, he's gonna pop." — Ron's talking head about Ben
jokes.setup: Ben is visibly straining to be nice while delivering bad news
jokes.punchline: Ron's precise diagnosis of Ben's psychological state, delivered with complete confidence
jokes.explanation: Ron's laconic wisdom is always entertaining. 'Little dude's wound so tight he's gonna pop' is vivid and accurate. Character-specific to Ron's observational remove from office politics.

dialogue.speaker: Tom
dialogue.line: Yeah, I simplified the whole thing. Everyone's a Golden Retriever now.

jokes.text: The spirit dogs chart has been replaced with spirit kangaroos, but there are barely any kangaroo species — so most people get the same one
jokes.setup: April has replaced the spirit dogs chart with spirit kangaroos
jokes.punchline: 'There aren't that many different types of kangaroos' — the game immediately fails because of a lack of kangaroo biodiversity
jokes.explanation: Good callback to the spirit dogs bit with a logical extension — April's attempt to one-up the game fails on a zoological technicality. The detail that Ron is a blue flyer and so is everyone else is a nice visual-comedy implication.

dialogue.speaker: Tom
dialogue.line: I have a two-step plan: step one, come up with idea; step two, execute idea.

dialogue.speaker: Leslie
dialogue.line: That's not a plan, that's a description of thinking.

dialogue.speaker: Tom
dialogue.line: Well, it works for me.

dialogue.speaker: Leslie
dialogue.line: I have 80 steps in my presentation system.

dialogue.speaker: Tom
dialogue.line: Of course you do.

jokes.text: "The Leslie Knope Project Preparedness Super System" — Tom has abandoned Leslie's elaborate presentation system
jokes.setup: Leslie asks which step Tom is at in her super system
jokes.punchline: Tom casually reveals they stopped doing it the moment she joined city council
jokes.explanation: Good character joke — the name alone ('The Leslie Knope Project Preparedness Super System') is funny. Tom's casual 'we kinda stopped doin' that' against Leslie's reverence for it is a nice contrast.

dialogue.speaker: Leslie
dialogue.line: It's not absurd! It's a perfectly logical system. Everything has its place, everything is color-coded, and cross-referenced with both alphabetical and chronological indices.

dialogue.speaker: Ron
dialogue.line: It's absurd.

dialogue.speaker: Leslie
dialogue.line: Well, the Pawnee Historical Society for Meticulous Record-Keeping and Binder Organization just gave me an award.

jokes.text: Tom's two-step presentation system: "Step one: Chill out a bit. Step two: Get up there and rip it."
jokes.setup: Leslie has just described her 80-step system developed over a decade
jokes.punchline: Tom's entire competing system is two steps, both of which are vibes-based
jokes.explanation: Excellent economy and character integration. The contrast between Leslie's exhaustive system and Tom's two-step vibes approach is the perfect expression of both characters. 'Rip it' as a step in a professional preparation system is legitimately funny. Justifies 8+ — it's precise, character-specific, and quotable.

dialogue.speaker: Leslie
dialogue.line: This is my domain. I know every inch of this office.

dialogue.speaker: Leslie
dialogue.line: I am in complete control—

dialogue.speaker: Leslie
dialogue.line: OW! What is this?!

jokes.text: Leslie quotes "the most thorough and, dare we say, at times, over-prepared presentation" from the Indiana blue ribbon panel on irrigation and drainage
jokes.setup: Leslie defends her super system
jokes.punchline: The most impressive endorsement she can cite comes from an obscure irrigation panel, and it includes the note that she was 'at times, over-prepared' — which she seems proud of
jokes.explanation: Funny character-specific detail — Leslie's most prized credential is an obscure panel's backhanded compliment, and she's completely unaware of its faint-praise quality. The specificity of 'irrigation and drainage' sells it.

dialogue.speaker: Ben
dialogue.line: Would you officers like some cheese?

dialogue.speaker: Police Officer
dialogue.line: Is this a bribe?

dialogue.speaker: Ben
dialogue.line: What? No, it's just cheese.

dialogue.speaker: Police Officer
dialogue.line: It feels like a bribe.

dialogue.speaker: Ben
dialogue.line: I'm going to jail, aren't I?

dialogue.speaker: Ben
dialogue.line: I'm surrendering. I'm going with you.

jokes.text: "You're the big dog around here." / "Big kangaroo."
jokes.setup: Tom defers to Leslie with a 'big dog' compliment
jokes.punchline: Ron corrects him — it's kangaroos now — with complete deadpan seriousness
jokes.explanation: Excellent callback — Ron, who seemed dismissive of the kangaroo game, has fully internalized it. His deadpan correction is funnier because he's the last person you'd expect to care about office spirit animals.

dialogue.speaker: April
dialogue.line: Wait, are you getting married?

dialogue.speaker: Chris
dialogue.line: What? No! Well, yes. But not because anyone's pregnant.

jokes.text: "Damn it! When did they put a lamp here?" — Leslie walks into a lamp after her triumphant speech about owning the parks game
jokes.setup: Leslie gives a confident speech about how 'this is still my house' and she 'invented this parks game'
jokes.punchline: She immediately walks into a lamp, proving she doesn't actually know the space anymore
jokes.explanation: Structurally perfect visual gag. The setup is Leslie's overconfident claim to ownership of the space; the physical punchline (lamp) immediately and literally disproves it. Perfect comic timing, earns its impact through excellent setup. Justifies 8+ for structure alone — this is how physical comedy should be built.

dialogue.speaker: Ann
dialogue.line: So that romantic moment when you planned the whole thing out?

dialogue.speaker: Chris
dialogue.line: Yeah, I didn't plan anything. I just showed up at your door with flowers I bought at a gas station and said 'We should probably get married.'

dialogue.speaker: Ann
dialogue.line: Those were from a gas station?

dialogue.speaker: Chris
dialogue.line: The only flowers they had left. They were next to the beef jerky.

jokes.text: "Ah, what can I do for you... for?" — Ben fumbles his greeting to the police
jokes.setup: Two police officers arrive at Ben's office about the cheese
jokes.punchline: Ben's nervous non-sentence 'what can I do for you... for?' signals immediate guilt
jokes.explanation: Nice cringe moment — Ben's immediate nervous breakdown over cheese smuggling. The dangling 'for?' is a good verbal stumble. Character-specific to Ben's anxious compliance.

dialogue.speaker: Leslie
dialogue.line: Tom, I know you didn't read my binder. I have a very specific security system. I replaced all the binding with hair from different animals. If you had actually read it, you'd be covered in hair from a llama, a chinchilla, and a very angry emu.

dialogue.speaker: Tom
dialogue.line: Leslie, that's insane.

dialogue.speaker: Leslie
dialogue.line: Is it? Is it insane, Tom? Because you're not covered in animal hair.

jokes.text: "Are you trying to bribe us?" / "No! Oh, God. I surrender."
jokes.setup: Ben tries to defuse the cheese situation by offering the officers some
jokes.punchline: The officers interpret it as a bribe; Ben, panicking, immediately surrenders
jokes.explanation: Ben's immediate 'I surrender' over cheese is perfect. His disposition toward rule-following makes the complete capitulation funny and character-specific. Escalation from cheese to bribery accusation to full surrender is well-paced.

dialogue.speaker: Ben
dialogue.line: What's going on? Why are there police officers here?

dialogue.speaker: Police Officer
dialogue.line: We need to talk to you about some serious charges.

dialogue.speaker: Ben
dialogue.line: Charges? What charges? I didn't do anything!

dialogue.speaker: Jerry
dialogue.line: Actually, Ben, you did.

dialogue.speaker: Ben
dialogue.line: Jerry? What are you—

dialogue.speaker: Police Officer
dialogue.line: We have photo documentation of everything.

dialogue.speaker: Tom
dialogue.line: Dude, you should see your face right now.

dialogue.speaker: Leslie
dialogue.line: Gotcha! This was all a prank! Look at these photos!

dialogue.speaker: Ben
dialogue.line: You guys... you got me. That was elaborate.

dialogue.speaker: April
dialogue.line: We've been planning this for weeks.

jokes.text: "Oh. No. This isn't a shotgun wedding, although, yes, she is pregnant, and, yes, we did just decide to get married today."
jokes.setup: The jeweler innocently asks about their plans, implying a shotgun wedding
jokes.punchline: Chris's denial immediately confirms every element of a shotgun wedding while technically insisting it isn't one
jokes.explanation: The classic denial-that-confirms structure, executed cleanly. Chris's oversharing and his need to qualify everything makes him the perfect character to deliver this. The rhythm of 'although, yes... and yes... but it's not' is well-constructed.

dialogue.speaker: Leslie
dialogue.line: Bisque? No. Absolutely not. Bisque is just a vehicle for cream and sadness. If I'm going to eat something that thick, it better be ice cream or regret.

dialogue.speaker: Stu
dialogue.line: It's a classic soup...

dialogue.speaker: Leslie
dialogue.line: It's a lie wrapped in a lobster shell. You know what? Retirement is off. We're doing this forever.

jokes.text: "And that's just for the rehearsal dinner." delivered twice — once by the jeweler's wife, once more for emphasis
jokes.setup: The jeweler's wife describes their months of wedding preparation
jokes.punchline: The list of elaborate preparations (invitations, table settings, color scheme, dance lessons) is revealed to be only for the rehearsal dinner — then repeated for maximum effect
jokes.explanation: Good escalation joke with satisfying structure. The repetition of 'that's just for the rehearsal dinner' doubles down correctly. Works as contrast to Chris and Ann's chaotic approach.

dialogue.speaker: Stu
dialogue.line: Using tiny glasses filled with hot stew instead of proper drinks

jokes.text: "All we did was punch 'jewelry store' into our car GPS. You remember that romantic moment, Chris? I was getting gas." / "No, I don't remember it."
jokes.setup: Ann sarcastically describes their romantic engagement journey
jokes.punchline: Chris doesn't even remember the 'moment' — he was getting gas, a detail that makes the non-memory worse
jokes.explanation: 'I was getting gas. No, I don't remember it.' is a great two-beat. The specificity of the gas station makes the non-memory funnier — there is literally nothing to remember. Clean, economic, true to the characters' chaotic courtship.

dialogue.speaker: Ann
dialogue.line: We've reached that level of intimacy where we can talk about anything. Like, I know exactly what Leslie does in the bathroom, and she knows my TV schedule.

dialogue.speaker: Leslie
dialogue.line: Ann, you really didn't need to bring that up.

dialogue.speaker: Ann
dialogue.line: No, it's sweet! Most couples don't get there. We're basically soulmates.

jokes.text: Leslie has booby-trapped her super system binder with a strand of hair to detect if Tom has read it
jokes.setup: Leslie asks if Tom reviewed the binder
jokes.punchline: She reveals she placed a strand of hair along the edge as a seal — Tom didn't open it
jokes.explanation: Highly character-specific — Leslie applying spy-thriller tradecraft to a work binder is the perfect expression of her obsessive thoroughness. The hair-seal detail is specific and absurd in exactly the right proportion. Justifies 8+ because it's a joke that literally could not be told about any other character.

dialogue.speaker: Larry
dialogue.line: You know, Ben, I've been here a long time. And I've learned that the best leaders are humble. They don't brag about their accomplishments. They let their work speak for itself.

dialogue.speaker: Larry
dialogue.line: Me? I'm just a simple guy who pushes papers and tries not to mess things up too bad.

jokes.text: Yeah, once you got on the city council, we kinda stopped doing that.
jokes.setup: Leslie enthusiastically asks Tom which step of her 80-step system he's on
jokes.punchline: Tom casually reveals they abandoned her entire system once she left — delivered with zero embarrassment
jokes.explanation: Tom's complete lack of guilt about abandoning Leslie's precious system is the joke. The casual delivery — 'yeah, we kinda stopped doing that' — is perfect. It's a slight against Leslie without any malice.

dialogue.speaker: Larry
dialogue.line: I pulled off the greatest prank in the history of pranks. I filled Jerry's office with balloons. Took me all night, but it was worth it.

dialogue.speaker: Jerry
dialogue.line: That's nice, Larry.

jokes.text: "Whose hair is that? It's brown." — Tom notices the hair is not Leslie's (she's blonde)
jokes.setup: Leslie reveals her hair-seal security system
jokes.punchline: Tom points out the hair is brown — Leslie is blonde — raising the question of whose hair she used
jokes.explanation: Perfect button to the binder joke. Three words that open up a disturbing question: Leslie sourced someone else's hair for this. The implication (Ron's elk hair) is funnier than stating it directly.

dialogue.speaker: Tom
dialogue.line: This mousse is incredible. It's got micro-nutrients and—wait, is mousse even still a thing? Do people use mousse anymore?

jokes.text: "And then you need two funny quotes and an inspirational one. You know, a classic ha-ha-hmm."
jokes.setup: Leslie lectures Tom on what a presentation needs
jokes.punchline: She's codified and trademarked a presentation structure down to emotional beats: ha-ha-hmm
jokes.explanation: 'A classic ha-ha-hmm' is an excellent coinage. It perfectly captures Leslie's tendency to systematize everything, and it's also a genuinely accurate description of how mediocre presentations work. High quotability.

dialogue.speaker: Chris
dialogue.line: Ann, will you marry me?

dialogue.speaker: Ann
dialogue.line: Yes! Oh my God, yes!

dialogue.speaker: Chris
dialogue.line: Wait, no, I changed my mind.

dialogue.speaker: Ann
dialogue.line: Oh thank God, me too.

jokes.text: "It's the most effective hair for binder security. You know that, Ron." — Leslie confirms she used Ron's elk hair
jokes.setup: Tom notices the brown hair on the binder
jokes.punchline: It's Ron's elk hair — and apparently this is established knowledge that Ron should be aware of
jokes.explanation: Outstanding callback payoff. 'Elk hair' is a perfect specific detail — it's absurd, it involves Ron's hunting hobby, and it implies Leslie regularly harvests his elk-hunting materials for office security. 'You know that, Ron' implies this is established procedure between them. Extremely high character integration for both Leslie and Ron. Justifies 8+ easily — it's original, structurally perfect, and deeply character-specific.

dialogue.speaker: Leslie
dialogue.line: Remember when Tom presented that idea about the laser pointer system and it went into his eye?

dialogue.speaker: Tom
dialogue.line: We don't talk about that.

dialogue.speaker: Leslie
dialogue.line: You lost vision in that eye for three weeks.

dialogue.speaker: Tom
dialogue.line: It came back eventually. Mostly.

jokes.text: I think you need to take a page out of my system and chill out a bit, okay? I got this.
jokes.setup: Leslie is spiraling about Tom's preparedness
jokes.punchline: Tom tells Leslie to follow Step 1 of his own system ('chill out a bit') — using his own terrible advice as wisdom
jokes.explanation: Good callback to Tom's system. The self-referential quality is amusing — Tom has complete confidence in his non-system.

dialogue.speaker: Tom
dialogue.line: Look, I didn't push Larry down the stairs. He fell because he was trying to sneak into my laser show without paying. He tripped on his own feet while running away from security.

dialogue.speaker: Larry
dialogue.line: That's not true! I was invited!

dialogue.speaker: Tom
dialogue.line: Larry, you were wearing a fake mustache and using the name 'Larry Gergich.' Your actual name is Larry Gergich.

jokes.text: But I think you're gonna fail, and you're a ticking time bomb. / What's that? / Nothing, good luck.
jokes.setup: Leslie says she 'trusts' Tom while clearly not trusting him
jokes.punchline: She accidentally mutters 'ticking time bomb' within earshot and then immediately pretends she said nothing
jokes.explanation: Leslie's inability to conceal her anxiety is played well. The 'Nothing, good luck' pivot is a classic sitcom beat but it's executed with good character specificity.

dialogue.speaker: Ben
dialogue.line: Okay everyone, I have an announcement. There's been a terrorist attack at City Hall. We need to evacuate immediately.

dialogue.speaker: April
dialogue.line: What? Where?

dialogue.speaker: Ben
dialogue.line: The east wing. There's a bomb. We have ten minutes. Also, the terrorists have taken hostages and they're demanding one million dollars and a helicopter to the airport.

dialogue.speaker: Jerry
dialogue.line: Oh my God!

dialogue.speaker: Ben
dialogue.line: And they've also poisoned the water supply. So don't drink anything. Also, there's a sniper on the roof. Everyone get down!

dialogue.speaker: Tom
dialogue.line: Ben, what are you doing?

dialogue.speaker: Ben
dialogue.line: And now the building is on fire. We have to repel down the side using the fire hose. Go, go, go!

jokes.text: "I cannot sit idly by and watch this terrible thing happen. I mean, I can barely sit idly by and watch good things happen."
jokes.setup: Leslie explains why she has to intervene in Tom's presentation
jokes.punchline: She clarifies that idly sitting by for ANY reason is impossible for her, undermining her justification
jokes.explanation: One of the best jokes in the episode. The self-correction ('I mean, I can barely sit idly by and watch good things happen') completely punctures her justification while being devastatingly accurate to her character. The structure is perfect: a justification that reveals its own absurdity. Extremely quotable. Firmly earns 8+ — this is the kind of confessional beat that exemplifies what Parks & Rec does best.

dialogue.speaker: April
dialogue.line: I'm going to kill you.

dialogue.speaker: Ben
dialogue.line: It's just fake blood, April. It washes right out.

dialogue.speaker: April
dialogue.line: Not you. I'm going to kill whoever told you that you're funny.

jokes.text: "I've never even jaywalked." / "Never?" / "I mean, I-I-- everyone does it sometimes. Just add that to the charges."
jokes.setup: Ben protests his law-abiding nature to the customs officers
jokes.punchline: He immediately contradicts himself on jaywalking and asks to have it added to his charges
jokes.explanation: Classic anxiety-spiral joke. Ben's rule-following nature collapsing under pressure, then immediately confessing to jaywalking and wanting it formally charged, is perfect character comedy. 'Just add that to the charges' is a great button.

dialogue.speaker: April
dialogue.line: This is the best day of my life.

jokes.text: "Seems you're wanted for tax fraud in Colorado?" / "I've never even been to Colorado. I mean, I had a layover in Denver once." / "Man, you can't keep your story straight, can you?"
jokes.setup: Police escalate the cheese arrest to tax fraud
jokes.punchline: Ben's 'I've never been to Colorado' is immediately self-refuted by 'I had a layover in Denver once' — the officer correctly notes he can't keep his story straight
jokes.explanation: Excellent escalation beat. The layover self-refutation is the joke — Denver IS Colorado, Ben. The officer's comment 'can't keep your story straight' validates the joke perfectly. Ben's anxiety is palpable and funny throughout this sequence.

dialogue.speaker: April
dialogue.line: He's three. And I know what you're doing. You're trying to have a fake emotional moment so I'll think you're sensitive. It won't work. I know you.

jokes.text: "You're pranked. You gotta see the stupid look on your face. Check this out. I took a picture."
jokes.setup: The entire elaborate cheese-arrest sequence has been building for three minutes
jokes.punchline: It was all a prank by Donna and April — the police were in on it
jokes.explanation: Good misdirection payoff on a sustained sequence. The reveal recontextualizes the entire cheese subplot. The picture-taking detail is a nice specific touch.

dialogue.speaker: Jewelry Store Owner
dialogue.line: Look, I've shown you 47 rings. You've rejected every single one.

dialogue.speaker: Ann
dialogue.line: What about that one?

dialogue.speaker: Jewelry Store Owner
dialogue.line: That's the same ring you said looked like 'a frozen tear.' Twice.

dialogue.speaker: Chris
dialogue.line: What if we got two rings? One for each hand?

dialogue.speaker: Jewelry Store Owner
dialogue.line: You know what? Take them all. Take the store. I'm done.

jokes.text: "Good one, makin' me think I was gonna like die in federal prison... Ah, that's super funny, you scamps."
jokes.setup: Ben has just been told it was all a prank
jokes.punchline: His shaken response — still processing federal prison fear — combined with the dated word 'scamps' is funny in its mismatch
jokes.explanation: 'You scamps' is a very funny word choice — it's the word of a man still too rattled to be appropriately angry. Character-specific to Ben's midwestern repression of genuine feelings.

dialogue.speaker: Leslie
dialogue.line: Stu is a master craftsman who has dedicated his life to the ancient art of stew-making. He works in conditions that would make a medieval peasant weep—hunched over a boiling cauldron for hours, his hands blistered from stirring an endless pot of root vegetables and mystery meat. He endures the acrid smoke that fills his lungs, the scalding splashes that mark his skin, the unbearable heat that beats down on him like a torturer's hammer.

jokes.text: "This calls for a toast. Susan? Stew flutes, please." — Leslie has prepared specialized stew-drinking vessels for the occasion
jokes.setup: Leslie wants to celebrate convincing Stu to stay
jokes.punchline: She has pre-arranged 'stew flutes' — the absurd specificity implies she had these made or sourced specifically for stew-toasting occasions
jokes.explanation: Stew flutes is a perfect absurdist Leslie detail. The casual name-drop implies entire infrastructure exists around this. Very character-specific — only Leslie would have custom vessels for a government stew vendor toast. Justifies 8+.

dialogue.speaker: Leslie
dialogue.line: Stew is just a way of saying 'I gave up on seasoning,' and 'I gave up on presentation.' It's really just a way of saying 'I gave up.' And when you're eating stew, you're basically eating someone's broken dreams in a bowl.

dialogue.speaker: Leslie
dialogue.line: And honestly, I think stew is what they serve in hell. Like, that's the thing they make you eat for all eternity—just lukewarm stew with mystery meat floating around in it.

dialogue.speaker: Leslie
dialogue.line: So basically, if you're making stew, you're either very poor or you're dead. And probably, you're dead.

jokes.text: The reaction to drinking hot stew from flutes — "Oh, my God. That's very hot."
jokes.setup: Stew flutes are presented and they toast
jokes.punchline: The stew is boiling hot in thin flute glasses — the impracticality of stew flutes immediately proven
jokes.explanation: Good physical payoff to the stew flutes joke. The obvious impracticality immediately demonstrated. Good callback completion.

dialogue.speaker: Stu
dialogue.line: I think I've made a terrible mistake.

jokes.text: "We could engrave '2014' or 'TBD.'" — jeweler offers to engrave the wedding date inside the ring
jokes.setup: The jeweler offers to engrave the date; Chris and Ann haven't discussed it
jokes.punchline: He casually offers 'TBD' as an engraving option, treating the couple's indecision as a normal engraving request
jokes.explanation: Nice dry joke from the jeweler. 'TBD' as a romantic inscription is funny in its bureaucratic coldness. Good economy.

dialogue.speaker: Leslie
dialogue.line: I think that went really well.

dialogue.speaker: Ben
dialogue.line: Leslie, you just threw a shoe at the mayor.

dialogue.speaker: Leslie
dialogue.line: Oh.

jokes.text: "You let me pee with the door open so I could watch the end of Grey's Anatomy. That was a fantastic season finale and a show that is literally a never-ending roller coaster of emotion."
jokes.setup: Chris argues they're already 'more married than most married people'
jokes.punchline: His evidence includes bathroom door intimacy combined with a completely sincere defense of Grey's Anatomy as a show
jokes.explanation: Two-part joke: the over-share of bathroom door policy as a relationship milestone, then Chris's unironic passion for Grey's Anatomy. 'A show that is literally a never-ending roller coaster of emotion' is very Chris Traeger — his over-earnest enthusiasm applied to prestige soap opera.

dialogue.speaker: Tom
dialogue.line: Treat yo'self.

jokes.text: "Theodore, we would like to return that ring. And get a refund, please."
jokes.setup: Chris has just convinced Ann they don't need a ring or wedding
jokes.punchline: He turns to the jeweler with complete composure and asks for a refund, as if returning a blender
jokes.explanation: Good tonal joke — the warmth of the romantic moment immediately followed by a transactional request. The name 'Theodore' also lands as slightly formal and funny.

jokes.text: "I was just printing out my minesweeper high score" — employee's reason for being near the printer when he found Ben's memo
jokes.setup: Employee comes to Ben with a warning memo
jokes.punchline: He reveals he was printing his Minesweeper high score — both explaining his presence and confirming why Ben's productivity rules are needed
jokes.explanation: Good specific detail — Minesweeper specifically (not just a game) implies government computer systems stuck in the late 1990s. Connects nicely to the earlier cell phone/shower break jokes about government productivity.

dialogue.speaker: Ron
dialogue.line: I hire the least qualified people. I do this intentionally. Because if I hire someone who has a passion for government and public service, I can't fire them for not doing a good job. It would be a personal betrayal. But if I hire someone who doesn't care, and they don't do a good job, I can just fire them and feel nothing. It's basic management.

jokes.text: "I know that you're the governor or whatever, and I'm just government junior."
jokes.setup: April is advising Ben not to send a warning memo after the prank
jokes.punchline: April characterizes their power dynamic with complete dismissiveness — 'governor or whatever'
jokes.explanation: Very April — her deliberate mangling of Ben's actual title ('city manager') to 'governor or whatever' expresses her characteristic DGAF attitude. Economy is excellent.

jokes.text: "I once did the best prank of all time. I dumped all of my boss's action figures into a fish tank." / "Yeah, that was me. And I didn't really like it."
jokes.setup: Tom tells Ben about the best prank he's ever done to help Ben learn
jokes.punchline: Ben was the boss with the action figures — and he tells Tom he didn't like it
jokes.explanation: Perfect two-beat joke. Tom brags about pranking his boss; his boss is the person he's talking to. Ben's flat 'And I didn't really like it' is a dry gut-punch. Both character voices are perfectly maintained. Tom's enthusiasm vs. Ben's understatement is a great comic dynamic. Justifies 8+.

jokes.text: "Who uses mousse still?" / "Oh, God. Leslie." / "Let's put our differences aside for a second. Friend to friend, do you still use mousse?" / "No, I use the juicy space thing--whatever you do."
jokes.setup: Tom and Leslie are arguing about the presentation; Tom insults her hair product
jokes.punchline: Ron — the least vain person in the room — breaks up a professional argument to solicit Leslie's hair product information
jokes.explanation: Ron secretly caring about hair products enough to interrupt a professional dispute is a great absurdist character-comedy moment. 'The juicy space thing' is a perfect vague product name for someone who doesn't pay attention to brand names but quietly uses them. Strong character integration for Ron.

jokes.text: No, I use the juicy space thing--whatever you do.
jokes.setup: Tom asked Ron about his hair products
jokes.punchline: Ron, who has presumably been asked about or observed Tom's hair product, refers to it as 'the juicy space thing' — Ron's complete indifference to product names while apparently being somewhat aware of Tom's routine
jokes.explanation: Ron calling hair product 'the juicy space thing' is a perfect Ron line — he refuses to engage with the commercial world on its own terms but does accidentally use Tom's product. 'Whatever you do' is the right dismissive button. Very high character integration.

jokes.text: "Yeah." / "I didn't think so." — Leslie's silent talking-head reaction after the argument
jokes.setup: Leslie and Tom have declared competing presentations
jokes.punchline: Leslie's talking head is just confident nodding and 'I didn't think so' — she's fully convinced she'll win
jokes.explanation: Functional reaction beat. Leslie's unearned confidence is a reliable character joke. Economy is the whole point here.

jokes.text: "On the other hand, there are some benefits to being married: Taxes, health insurance, and I don't have to feel weird when hotel employees call me 'Mr. Perkins.'"
jokes.setup: Chris and Ann debate whether to get married
jokes.punchline: Chris's reasons for marriage include a hotel staff embarrassment that's clearly a persistent issue for him
jokes.explanation: The 'Mr. Perkins' detail is the joke — it implies this has happened multiple times and bothers him more than he's admitting. Good escalation from taxes to very specific hotel embarrassment. Character-specific to Chris's fitness/health/name consciousness.

jokes.text: "Yeah, that makes me feel weird too." — Ann's response to being called Mr. Perkins
jokes.setup: Chris says he feels weird being called 'Mr. Perkins'
jokes.punchline: Ann also feels weird about her own last name being used that way — brief but perfect
jokes.explanation: Good reaction beat — Ann's secondary weirdness about her own name being used for him adds a layer. Economy is nearly perfect.

jokes.text: "Ann Perkins, will you marry me?" / "I don't know!" / "Me either!" / "Maybe let's not?" / "Yeah, I think maybe not." / "Okay. Ring's yours again. Hello?" / "Actually, we don't want the ring." / "Unbelievable."
jokes.setup: Chris spontaneously proposes again in the jewelry store
jokes.punchline: Neither of them knows, they jointly decide not to, the jeweler tries to recover the sale, they decline again — all in about 20 seconds
jokes.explanation: Great escalating callback. The jeweler's 'Hello?' and 'Unbelievable' are the perfect reactions to being whipsawed through three ring decisions. The mutual simultaneous uncertainty ('I don't know!' 'Me either!') is very charming. Structure builds to the jeweler's exasperation perfectly.

jokes.text: Ben revealing his prank plan: ski masks, fake kidnapping, squibs, divers, a van driven into a river — all to look like a hero to Donna and April
jokes.setup: Ben is about to pull a prank, guided by Tom. He's about to reveal what he's planned.
jokes.punchline: The plan is catastrophically over-elaborate for a workplace prank: ski mask kidnappers, fake blood squibs, van into river, scuba divers
jokes.explanation: Ben's extreme over-engineering of what should be a simple prank is perfect character comedy — his nerd-brain takes a social problem and treats it like a military operation. Each escalation (ski masks → squibs → van into river → divers) is funnier than the last. The planned hero pose 'Hey, you get pranked much?' is great. Justifies 8+.

jokes.text: "Oh, my God. You got blood all over me." — Ben accidentally triggers the squibs and covers Donna in fake blood
jokes.setup: Ben is confessing he was about to prank them and that he has squibs
jokes.punchline: He accidentally triggers the squibs mid-confession, covering Donna in fake blood
jokes.explanation: Perfect physical payoff to the escalating prank plan. The accidental triggering mid-confession is classic farce structure — the elaborate scheme backfires precisely when Ben is trying to avoid it. 'You got blood all over me' as Donna's flat response is excellent.

jokes.text: Ben, that was amazing. / Really? / Best prank ever.
jokes.setup: Ben accidentally executed a prank while confessing he was cancelling his prank
jokes.punchline: April — who hates almost everything — declares it 'best prank ever,' validating a disaster as success
jokes.explanation: April's approval is meaningful precisely because she gives it so rarely. The implication that accidentally shooting fake blood during a confession IS the best prank approach is an absurdist inversion. Ben's 'Really?' — genuinely seeking validation — is a nice beat.

jokes.text: "Ben, that was amazing." / "Really?" / "Best prank ever." — Donna and April love the accidental squib explosion
jokes.setup: Ben is mortified by accidentally triggering the squibs
jokes.punchline: Donna and April are delighted — the unintentional bloodbath was funnier than any planned prank
jokes.explanation: Nice irony close — Ben's careful planning is rejected but his accident succeeds. Ties off the prank arc satisfyingly.

jokes.text: "I'm sorry, buddy, daddy can't get home to tuck you in." — Chris on the phone in the jewelry store; "Oh, how old is your son?" / "Just pick a thing."
jokes.setup: Chris is on the phone at a tender parenting moment
jokes.punchline: Ann, exasperated by his emotional tangents during their jewelry decisions, tells him 'Just pick a thing'
jokes.explanation: Functional character beat. Ann's patience with Chris's emotional digressions. 'Just pick a thing' is good Ann characterization.

jokes.text: "And when we did date, we broke up, but you didn't realize it, and that was very embarrassing for you."
jokes.setup: Ann is narrating the unconventional story of their relationship
jokes.punchline: She casually includes the detail that Chris didn't realize they had broken up — and notes it was 'very embarrassing for you' with complete calm
jokes.explanation: Great character-specific dig. The flat 'very embarrassing for you' is both caring and cutting — Ann is comfortable enough with the story to be honest in front of the jeweler. Character integration is high for both: Chris's emotional obliviousness and Ann's candor.

jokes.text: "Yeah, let's maybe not talk about that part right now." — Chris's embarrassed response to the breakup detail
jokes.setup: Ann has just publicly revealed Chris didn't know they were broken up
jokes.punchline: Chris requests not discussing it — in front of a stranger, mid-locket purchase
jokes.explanation: Functional reaction beat. Good button to joke #61 but doesn't add much beyond confirming Chris's embarrassment.

jokes.text: "How much?" / "Just take it and get outta here." — jeweler gives them the locket for free just to end the transaction
jokes.setup: After multiple ring purchases, returns, and decision reversals, Chris asks the price of the locket
jokes.punchline: The jeweler just gives it to them for free — he's done with this couple
jokes.explanation: Perfect close to the jewelry store subplot. The jeweler's exasperation reaching the point where he'd rather lose money than continue the interaction is a great payoff. 'Just take it and get outta here' is a beautifully economical final line for this arc.

jokes.text: Leslie's presentation describes Stu as 'bent over a boiling cauldron of steaming, bubbling meat' and wanting to bury him 'under that shed'
jokes.setup: Leslie is making an enthusiastic case for renewing Stu's stew lease
jokes.punchline: Her advocacy becomes increasingly grim — the stew stand sounds like a hellscape, and she wants him to work there until he dies and is buried on premises
jokes.explanation: This is a standout joke. Leslie's relentless advocacy tips into accidentally horrifying territory — her endorsement of Stu is actually an endorsement of physical misery and eventual workplace death. 'Pungent beef smoothies' and 'bury him under that shed' are inspired language choices. The obliviousness makes it funnier. Justifies 8+ strongly.

jokes.text: "I think I've made a terrible mistake." — Stu's talking head after Leslie's presentation
jokes.setup: Leslie has just described Stu's future as 'pungent beef smoothies until we bury him under that shed'
jokes.punchline: Stu quietly realizes he should have retired
jokes.explanation: Perfect button to joke #64. The understatement ('terrible mistake') following Leslie's accidentally horrifying pitch is a great deadpan payoff. Economy is nearly perfect.

jokes.text: "Hey. Rip it." — Tom's entire pre-presentation ritual
jokes.setup: Tom is called up to present
jokes.punchline: His entire prep is the word 'Rip it' to himself — the full execution of his two-step system
jokes.explanation: Perfect callback payoff to the two-step system joke. Two words completing a full circle: Tom described his system as 'chill out a bit, then rip it' — and we see exactly that in action. The economy is extraordinary. This is how callbacks should work. Justifies 8+.

jokes.text: Tom has personalized lemonade cups for individual committee members — "Has my name on it" / "Yes it does. Classic for you, Carter." / "Darva, yours is a pink lemonade. I know you love that."
jokes.setup: Tom asks who likes laser shows and tells people to check under their seats
jokes.punchline: He's prepared personalized lemonades for each committee member — knowing their individual preferences — which is simultaneously impressive and deeply Tom
jokes.explanation: This joke validates Tom's character growth while still being funny. He's researched each committee member's preferences — which is more preparation than Leslie's system would have required. 'Classic for you, Carter' implies ongoing research into these people. Strong character integration.

jokes.text: There's nothing more American than lemonade. Just sayin' the word makes you wanna drink some. And now you can. Check under your seats.
jokes.setup: Tom opens his presentation
jokes.punchline: He has personally put lemonade under each committee member's seat — a showman's move that both validates his 'presentation over content' philosophy and actually works
jokes.explanation: Tom's 'check under your seats' move — turning a business presentation into a talk-show moment — is exactly what Tom would do. 'Just sayin' the word makes you wanna drink some' is an effective (if slightly cheesy) opener that works precisely because Tom believes it completely.

jokes.text: "Look, guys, I'm sorry about all the new rules, but I want you to like me. But I also really need you to respect me." / "I respect you, little buddy. Come here." / "Mm, respect noogie."
jokes.setup: Ben gives a sincere speech about wanting respect and likability
jokes.punchline: Donna's response is to give him a 'respect noogie' — the least dignified form of affection
jokes.explanation: The 'respect noogie' coinage is good. The word 'noogie' itself is funny, and naming the noogie as an act of respect makes it better. Donna calling him 'little buddy' also lands well.

jokes.text: Look, guys, I'm sorry about all the new rules, but--you know, I want you to like me. But I-I also really need you to respect me. / I respect you, little buddy. Come here. / Mm, respect noogie. Ah!
jokes.setup: Ben gives a sincere, vulnerable speech about wanting respect
jokes.punchline: Tom immediately gives him a 'respect noogie' — demonstrating respect through exactly the kind of undignified physical contact that undermines the speech
jokes.explanation: 'Respect noogie' is an excellent coinage — Tom inventing a new category of physical affection that nominally honors Ben's request while doing the opposite. The immediate shift from Ben's emotional vulnerability to Tom giving him a noogie is a perfect tonal reversal.

jokes.text: "♪ R-e-s-p-e-g-c" / "Well, that's actually not how respect is spelled." / "According to Urethra Franklin, that's exactly how it's spelled."
jokes.setup: April starts singing Aretha Franklin's 'Respect'
jokes.punchline: She misspells it; Ben corrects her; she credits 'Urethra Franklin' as her source
jokes.explanation: One of the best jokes in the episode. 'Urethra Franklin' is a wordplay pun that is both juvenile and perfectly executed — the name swap is anatomically specific in a way that makes it funnier than a random substitution. April's deadpan defense of the misspelling ('that's exactly how she spells it') commits fully to the bit. High quotability, strong character integration (April would absolutely both know and misattribute this), and the Ben correction feeding into it is structurally tight. Justifies 8+ easily.

jokes.text: "Here's a little gift for you for believing in me." / "It's a gel-based hair serum." / "Enough with the mousse, for real."
jokes.setup: Tom thanks Ben for believing in him
jokes.punchline: The gift is a hair product — callback to the mousse argument — and Tom refuses to let it go
jokes.explanation: Good callback close to the mousse subplot. Tom's gift being a hair product is both thoughtful (in Tom's way) and a continuation of the joke. 'Enough with the mousse, for real' is a good button.

jokes.text: "No. We do not." — Ron's answer when Leslie asks if the department even needs her anymore
jokes.setup: Leslie reflects warmly on Tom and April's growth, then asks if the department needs her anymore
jokes.punchline: Ron answers immediately and without qualification: No
jokes.explanation: Classic Ron Swanson economy. She asks a sincere, emotionally loaded question; he answers with complete bluntness and no hesitation. The 'No. We do not.' — with the formal pronoun clarification — is even funnier than a simple 'No.' It's both a gut punch and an act of love in Ron's language. Justifies 8+ through perfect character integration and economy.

jokes.text: April and Tom started out as two of the most apathetic people I had ever met. It's why I hired them.
jokes.setup: Ron is reflecting on how the department has evolved
jokes.punchline: 'It's why I hired them' — Ron hired them for their apathy because he wanted people who wouldn't do anything, which is his ideal government office
jokes.explanation: One of the episode's best Ron jokes. The revelation that he hired April and Tom specifically for their apathy — because his ideal government office is one that does as little as possible — is a perfect crystallization of Ron's philosophy. 'It's why I hired them' lands as both a punchline and a complete worldview statement. Highly quotable, strong economy.

jokes.text: "Then you betrayed me and turned them into efficient and caring government employees."
jokes.setup: Ron explains he hired April and Tom because they were apathetic
jokes.punchline: He calls Leslie's positive influence on them a 'betrayal' — because they're no longer the slackers he wanted
jokes.explanation: Outstanding character joke. Ron's libertarian/anti-government worldview means that making good government employees is a form of betrayal. 'Efficient and caring government employees' delivered as an accusation is deeply Ron. This line works on comedy and character simultaneously. Firmly 8+.

jokes.text: "Was that a death threat?" — Leslie's response to Ron's speech about her not being here forever
jokes.setup: Ron gives a sincere speech about Leslie's legacy and moving on to bigger things
jokes.punchline: Leslie interprets the poetic speech as a death threat
jokes.explanation: Good puncturing of Ron's rare moment of sentimentality. Leslie's anxiety reading 'you won't be here forever' as a death threat is paranoid and funny. The straight-man/clown reversal — Ron being sincere while Leslie panics — is a nice switch from their usual dynamic.

jokes.text: "God help me — you've built a well-functioning government agency."
jokes.setup: Ron is giving Leslie his highest compliment
jokes.punchline: For Ron, 'a well-functioning government agency' is something he'd only admit under duress — hence 'God help me'
jokes.explanation: This is the emotional and comedic peak of the episode. 'God help me' before complimenting government is perfect Ron — it's the highest praise he can give while simultaneously suffering for saying it. The joke is both funny and genuinely moving, which is the Parks & Rec sweet spot. Strong 8+, possibly the best Ron joke in the episode.

jokes.text: Leslie receives Pawnee's government employee of the month — and her emotional reaction is so overwhelming the scene just cuts to the credits before it ends
jokes.setup: Ron reveals Leslie has received Employee of the Month for creating Tom's financially successful position
jokes.punchline: Leslie's reaction is so extended and overwhelming that the episode literally cannot contain it — we cut before she finishes
jokes.explanation: Meta-structural joke — the comedic choice is the edit itself. Leslie's over-the-top emotional response is so reliably excessive that the show jokes by cutting away before it concludes. This is good mockumentary structure: the comedy is in the absence. High character integration.

tmdb_overview: Leslie fights with Ben over questionable sales techniques at the local farmers market. Ann searches for a way to vent about the annoying aspects of pregnancy, while April supports Andy in a new creative venture.
insight: Understated ensemble episode coasts on character chemistry despite below-season-average joke density.
